name: Baekho
shortDescription: Baekho, the White Tiger, is a divine guardian of the West in Korean mythology, symbolizing strength, courage, and protection.
description: Baekho, meaning 'White Tiger,' is a prominent figure in Korean mythology, revered as one of the four directional guardians. Representing the West, Baekho embodies strength, courage, and the protection of the cardinal direction it oversees. Its origins are deeply rooted in ancient Korean beliefs about the cosmos and the spiritual significance of animals. As a divine beast, Baekho is often depicted in murals and folklore, serving as a symbol of power and a deterrent against evil spirits. The White Tiger's association with the West connects it to themes of autumn, metal, and the element of wind, further solidifying its role in the Korean cosmological framework. It is considered a king of all beasts and is said to only appear when the ruler reigns with absolute virtue, or when peace reigns in the world. The Baekho is not merely a fearsome predator but a benevolent guardian, ensuring balance and harmony.
subtitle: Guardian of the West, Tiger of Virtue
habitat: Mountains and forests of the West
appearance: Baekho is a majestic white tiger, distinguished by its pristine fur and piercing gaze. Its size is often depicted as larger than a normal tiger, emphasizing its divine status. Its stripes, though subtle, are said to glow faintly in the dark.

extendedContent.title: Origins & Mythology
extendedContent.content: The origins of Baekho are intertwined with ancient Korean shamanistic beliefs and the adoption of Chinese cosmological principles. The concept of the Four Symbols (Sasin), including the White Tiger of the West, was integrated into Korean culture, influencing art, architecture, and religious practices. Myths surrounding Baekho often depict it as a protector of tombs and sacred sites, warding off malevolent spirits. Legends also tell of Baekho appearing to righteous rulers, signifying their virtuous reign and the prosperity of the kingdom. The White Tiger is believed to embody the yin energy, representing the feminine and passive aspects of the universe, balancing the yang energy of other directional guardians.

extendedContent.title: Role & Significance
extendedContent.content: Baekho plays a crucial role in maintaining cosmic balance and protecting the Western cardinal direction. Its presence is considered auspicious, bringing peace, prosperity, and good fortune. In traditional Korean geomancy (pungsu), the White Tiger's position is carefully considered when selecting locations for buildings and tombs to ensure harmony with the surrounding environment. Baekho is also revered as a symbol of military prowess and courage, often depicted on banners and armor to inspire warriors. Its image is invoked in rituals and ceremonies to invoke protection and ward off evil influences. The White Tiger is a powerful symbol of authority, justice, and the unwavering defense of the righteous.

extendedContent.title: Symbolism & Interpretation
extendedContent.content: The white color of Baekho symbolizes purity, righteousness, and the metal element associated with the West. Its association with autumn represents the season of harvest and reflection, a time for gathering resources and preparing for the future. The White Tiger's role as a guardian reflects the importance of protecting boundaries and maintaining order, both in the physical and spiritual realms. Its presence is a reminder of the constant struggle between good and evil, and the need for vigilance against malevolent forces. The White Tiger also represents the strength and resilience of the Korean people, their ability to overcome adversity and uphold their values in the face of challenges. The number seven is also associated with the Baekho, a representation of the stars within the constellation that represents the tiger.

extendedContent.title: Legacy & Influence
extendedContent.content: Baekho's legacy continues to resonate in modern Korean culture, appearing in art, literature, and popular media. Its image is often used in branding and advertising to convey qualities of strength, reliability, and trustworthiness. The White Tiger serves as a mascot for sports teams and other organizations, embodying the spirit of competition and the pursuit of excellence. In contemporary Korean shamanism, Baekho is still invoked in rituals and ceremonies, maintaining its role as a protector and guardian. The enduring presence of Baekho in Korean society reflects the deep-seated respect for tradition and the enduring power of mythology to shape cultural identity. The PyeongChang 2018 Winter Olympics used a white tiger named Soohorang as its mascot, further cementing the legacy of the Baekho.

cross_cultural_parallels.name: Baihu
cross_cultural_parallels.similarity: The White Tiger of the West in Chinese mythology, sharing similar attributes and symbolism.

cross_cultural_parallels.name: Byakko
cross_cultural_parallels.similarity: The White Tiger of the West in Japanese mythology, adapted from Chinese beliefs.

companions.name: Cheongnyong
companions.description: The Azure Dragon of the East, representing the opposite direction and balancing Baekho's power.

companions.name: Jujak
companions.description: The Vermilion Bird of the South, another of the Four Symbols, representing fire and summer.

companions.name: Hyeonmu
companions.description: The Black Turtle of the North, the final of the Four Symbols, representing water and winter.

worshipPractices.name: Offerings at shrines
worshipPractices.description: Small shrines are sometimes erected in honor of the Baekho, where offerings of food and drink are left to seek its protection.

worshipPractices.name: Invocation in rituals
worshipPractices.description: Shamans invoke the name and power of Baekho during rituals to ward off evil spirits and bring good fortune.

festivals.name: Autumn Harvest Festival (Chuseok)
festivals.description: While not directly dedicated to Baekho, the festival celebrates the harvest season associated with the West and the White Tiger's domain.

cultural.modernLegacy: Baekho continues to appear in modern Korean art, literature, and popular culture, serving as a symbol of strength, protection, and national identity.
